title: The Connected Sayings
hook: thousands of short discourses gathered by topic

segments.voice: Yesterday: the short books closed. Your line: short and deep. Today a new block begins, with a very different kind of book.

A hardware store doesn't shelve things by size. Hinges go with hinges, nails with nails, paint with paint, big or small. Walk in needing one little bracket and you know which aisle to try. The early Buddhist community had thousands of short teachings to remember, and at some point someone sorted a great many of them into aisles by topic. That sorted store is the third great collection of the Pali canon: the Samyutta Nikaya.
screen: `A HARDWARE STORE.` → `SORTED BY KIND, NOT SIZE.` → `THOUSANDS OF TEACHINGS, BY TOPIC.`

segments.voice: Samyutta means connected, or yoked together, and nikaya means a collection. So, the Connected Sayings: discourses yoked together by their subject. The Long Discourses were sorted by length. The Middle-Length, more or less by length too. The Samyutta is sorted by kind. All the conversations with devas go in one chapter. All the meetings with Mara in another. The talks with King Pasenadi together; the teachings on feeling, on the five heaps, on the six senses, on the path. There are fifty-six of these chapters, gathered into five books. The first is the book with verses, full of short poems and questions from gods, kings and nuns. The others take on the great themes: how things arise from causes, the heaps, the senses, and finally the path and the four noble truths. Many of the discourses are tiny, a few lines, sometimes just a simile. Here's one, paraphrased, from the chapter on breakthrough. The Buddha picks up a little dust on the tip of his fingernail and asks the monks: which is more, this dust or the great earth? The earth, sir, of course. In the same way, he says, for a disciple who has truly seen the teaching, the suffering already ended is like the earth. What's left is like the dust on a fingernail. That's the whole discourse. Small, sorted, and easy to find again. For the next weeks, one aisle at a time.
screen: `SAMYUTTA: YOKED TOGETHER` · `SORTED BY KIND, NOT LENGTH` · `FIFTY-SIX CHAPTERS, FIVE BOOKS` · `DUST ON A FINGERNAIL` · then, large: `GATHERED BY KIND.`

segments.voice: Hold up one hand, look at a fingernail, and imagine a few grains of dust on its tip; then let the mind open out to the ground under you, the street, the whole earth, and feel the difference in size. Think of a difficulty you've already come through, something that once felt enormous and is behind you, and let it be the earth. Whatever is still hard today, let it, for now, be the dust.
Samyutta Nikaya. The Connected Sayings: thousands of short discourses, yoked together by topic into fifty-six chapters and five books. Today's word.
Your line: gathered by kind. Thousands of small teachings, each on its own shelf. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Theravada monastics and lay students study the Samyutta Nikaya chapter by chapter, and teachers draw short similes from it for talks, since its discourses are grouped by topic.

chat.says: How is the Samyutta Nikaya different from the other big collections?
options: It's sorted by kind: discourses yoked together by subject, not by length.
It holds only the Buddha's longest talks, one complete journey per book.
It's a commentary written centuries later to explain the other books.

notes: Block F opens. Confirm: 56 samyuttas in five vaggas (Sagatha, Nidana, Khandha, Salayatana, Maha); 'third great collection' follows the usual order DN, MN, SN, AN.

SN 13.1 (Abhisamaya Samyutta, the fingernail) paraphrased; confirm the simile (a little dust on the fingernail versus the great earth; for a noble disciple accomplished in view, the suffering destroyed is far greater than what remains, at most seven more lives).
The Chinese Samyuktagama parallel is a standard scholarly note.
The Middle-Length Discourses being 'more or less by length' is a simplification; a Keeper may prefer different wording.
